blocks.x: John Perhonas It's all over the back, Sam. Yeah. Mm-hmm. My name is John Perhonas, and I'm from the American Studies Program at the University of Minnesota. Next to me is Dick Allen, Curator of the Jazz Archives at Tulane University. And we are talking of William Russell at his home on Orleans Street in New Orleans. Today is February 16, 1976, George Washington's Birthday. Officially. Officially. We don't know whether it is or not. Anyway, I'd like to ask Bill Russell something about his name, because I think that will lead into something about his musical background. Is William Russell your real name?

It's my first name and second name. I was born and also William Wagner, and then when I began writing music music. Roughly around 1930, we'll say. I changed it as a pen name, just using my middle name and first name then.
Nice. Did you not want to confuse your name with the great composer?

Yeah, it wasn't exactly confusing. It makes you look too much like a phony. It's like if you say, if your name was Henry Shakespeare and you started to write plays, they'd say, what's this guy trying to do? You know, kiddus or something?
I'm going to ask a real killer of a question. How did you ever get interested in jazz?

Well, I heard music when I was a kid, of course, like on the river boats and other places around town. I was raised in a small town on the Mississippi River. There wasn't any real jazz bands, but there used to be a few piano players, and especially on the boats I'd hear jazz. But I didn't really try to listen to it. I used to have the idea that it was... In fact, my violin teacher told me, don't try to play any of that music. It'll, you know, corrupt your style. I'll revile it. So, I did listen to records, especially when I went to New York I began hearing records. Sometimes out on the street, like on Broadway, I remember standing there listening to some jazz records, which always fascinated me. And that was a sort of exciting thing. I was a very good one. It just fascinated me. And that was, say, 1928-29, along that period. And then I got interested. I picked up the first record I really ever picked up was a Jelly Roll Martin, Shoeshiners Drag. That would be in 1929. And I liked that so well. I began trying to get other records of his. Then I heard about Louis Armstrong and King Oliver, and started trying to find their records. That was the passion of my violin. That was the Depression that started then. You could pick up, well, Paramount's in New York for three cents a piece, they sold them.
Where'd you get, where would you get?

A place called Bloomfields on 14th Street had bought out, supposedly, 150,000 Paramounts, some bankrupt distributor or something, I guess it was. John Hammond went through those first. He was just a kid then, probably high school or maybe going to Yale at that time. And that's where he got a lot of his collection. That's where he found, say, the Medlux Lewis record and those things that he began looking for Medlux Lewis a few years later before he found him. So they sold those for three cents a piece. And then later they raised the price to 35 cents. But they had dozens of different Mauraenies and all the old Paramounts, you might say. Not the real old blue label. They were all black label.
Were these records brought into this store by record collectors? Or were they just there?

Well, it was everything from sporting goods and cameras. It was up on the second floor where they had this whole big room full of records. Later they moved most of them downstairs when they would sell them.
To your recollection, is Hammond one of the first collectors of early jazz?

He would be one of the earliest that I ever met and that I knew of. But there had been, like Charles Smith had known a few people at Princeton, I know, that had collected records. Probably in the twenties even. Did Charlie Smith go to school with him? I don't know that he went to Princeton either. But there were a few people from there, I remember, that he talked about.
I think Fred Ramsey said that he had, you know, relatively little education. Possibly. But he was, you know, just well educated as far as self-education.
Yeah, as far as reading and all that goes. No, I never did know his background, if he went to college at all either.
Did you know Fred Ramsey at, he was a graduate of Princeton I think.

Yeah, I met him in 1938. And soon after that he got the idea of, he worked for Harcourt Brace in the textbook department at that time. And talked his boss into having this anthology, Jazzmen, it turned out to be. So I had known him from around, we had what we called a hot record exchange. A friend of mine, Steve Smith, had started it in February of 36, 1936. In New York City? Yeah, in New York. He had been an artist drawing covers for, well like Wild West magazines, you know. It looked like gun smoke. The first time I met him, he went up to his house, he had an unfinished painting it was. He did it in oil, I think even. On the easel. And over several years later, that thing was still there. He got interested in jazz and started this hot record exchange. He never did go back to painting. And his wife fortunately had a job as a secretary. And because we didn't have any income from the hot record exchange, we used that mostly just to improve our own collections. And traded and sold a few, you know, to pay for the expenses of digging up new lots of records. So, that was in 1936 that he started that. So it would be soon after that, maybe the next year or so I met Ramsey. Might have been early in 38 even. And met Charles Smith about 1936 I guess.
Now you met all these people in New York. Yeah.

You were living in New York at the time. Yes, I lived in New York from 1929 on far. What were you doing in New York? I went there first to study at Columbia University and study violin. And I stayed around there. Did part time teaching. And during the Depression I traveled with a Chinese shadow play company. Played Chinese instruments. We traveled all over the country. For about six or seven years I did that.
And you continued your interest in collecting records at that time.

Every town that I'd go into in place of the rest of them would maybe go and eat lunch and I'd grab a banana and start going from one junk store to another second hand stores. And occasionally in those days you could go to a new music store. And they had brand new records they were selling out for ten cents a piece.
Were you looking for certain artists or...?

Just everything that had to do with the so called hot jazz as we called it then. At that time not all the people were known but I was especially interested in Louis Armstrong and other New Orleans people. And I tried to get all the Louis. At that time we didn't even know which ones Louis was on. Like say we knew he was on a bunch of the Fletcher Hendersons. So I'd pick up every Henderson I'd see and we'd take it home and listen to it and try to see if we could hear Louis on it.
Was there any written guides at that time that you would have had to go by?

The first book that came out that I ever saw was Schleman or Schleman, how do you pronounce it? Schleman, that sounds like a famous name. It's an English show. It came out about 1936 and then Delaunay came out about the next year or so I'd say. Around 37. These were discographies. So yeah the discography, the first edition of that. So and then George, not George Haver, at first Marshall Stearns was running a column in Downbeat. And sort of a history of jazz as he called it. So he would sometimes talk about records too.
He was in New York I think.
He was in Yale at that time. Oh I see.
Of course there hadn't been written, hadn't been any full length book written on the subject of jazz.

Well, yeah. Go Fan had written the book. And also Panassier's book came out I think in this country about 1936. Maybe even 35, I'd have to look up the date. But there's no other American books at least had been written. I think Hobson's was about the first one really. A full length book of Wilder Hobson. And that was more like 1938 I guess.

Well, Jazzmen is known outside of, well in academic circles where I'm from as the first definitive book on American jazz. That is from the point of view of the musicians. Yeah, well it wasn't exactly definitive.
At least we did.
The first to bring to the attention of national publics New Orleans music and Chicago.
Yeah, in some ways that is true. The fact that we actually called a section of it on New Orleans you know.
And at that, of course, were you living in New Orleans or did you come down here?

No, I never got here until 1937 for the first time. I see. And I'd made a couple trips, just very quick trips here once. The first time I was traveling with the Red Gate Shadowplayers, the Chinese Shadowplay. And I just spent one day here. Mostly a night it was actually. And then the next year I made two trips here with a friend, sort of record hunting trips. We went as far as Florida and Texas to the west. He was from Philadelphia. I just saw him in Bermuda last month. I was surprised. A fellow by the name of Park Breck, who was a newspaper reporter. So we made two trips and we stopped here. And we didn't hear much music with people like Tom Brown. No, I did get to hear him then. He was playing with Raymond Burke. Out at a place called the Derby Inn, I believe it is. The Dandy Inn.
Dandy Inn.
Yeah, that's at Dandy Inn. Out on the Jefferson Davis Parkway. Big barn like place. But otherwise I didn't spend much time here until 1942 about.

Well, there's a chapter in Jasmine called New Orleans Music. Yeah. Which you did with Stephen Smith. I think you did that. Now, how did you and he decide to do it together? And how did your research? I don't know who suggested that we do it together.

Steve is much interested in New Orleans Music too, of course. We were partners in the Hot Record Exchange. So, actually at that time he got the idea of opening a store then, a retail store, which didn't open until 1939. Right. But he was very busy organizing things. And actually didn't have time really to work on that chapter except his wife did most of the work and she did a lot of the research. Steve and she would go around and interview people. I'd made a couple of trips to Chicago. We even got an advance. I think that Ramsey got about a, oh, it was roughly a $200 advance from Harcourt. And there were about eight people. So I think we each got a $30 advance royalty deal out of it. So, I made one trip to Chicago. And Ramsey gave me some or maybe all of his money to go there and do research on King Oliver too. He had to do the King Oliver chapter.
That's right.
He did that.
So you researched the King Oliver chapter?

Partly. I wouldn't say that. Just the people in Chicago. Right. Because after all, Oliver did most of his important recording and you might say later playing in Chicago. So a lot of people there knew him and several members of the band were still living like, of course, Lil and Louie. And Bill Johnson, Dodds, both the Dodds brothers. So Ramsey couldn't get away from his job at Harcourt. So I did that work for him. All that we could. Unfortunately, no tape machines then. Just had to do it longhand. And I'd take the notes back to New York and try to enlarge a little bit on them. And Steve Smith's wife would type it out. She was a good secretary, as I mentioned before. And would type out the notes then for us. And she and Steve interviewed people in New York, such as Zutty Singleton and Sidney Bechet and a few others from New Orleans were there. So, but when it got time to really write out the stuff, Steve was too busy. So I just took all the notes and material and did the actual writing of it. But I'm not trying to say that Steve really fell down on the job because he was busy with those other things which had to be done then. So then I also wrote the Louis Armstrong chapter.
Was Steve Smith's wife really interested and involved in things?

Well yeah, she was much interested in jazz too. She liked it. What was her name? Lee Smith. Lee Smith. L-E-E. Strange name in a way for a girl. But I guess I know it was Lee Wiley and other people named that I can think of.

But anyway, Jelly was pretty disgusted when he saw the book and that he didn't get any more attention than he did.
When did Jelly do the Library of Congress records? What year was that?
That was in the spring of 1938.
So that was...

So there wasn't, you see, much interest there either. I mean, people didn't even know Jelly was there. A fellow by the name of Sidney Martin was probably the first one that discovered that Jelly was in Washington. And he wrote a little piece, maybe only a couple of inches long column or so on Jelly in Downbeat. And Charles Smith was down there soon after that working for the government. And anyway, I don't know who suggested, it might be that it was Sidney Martin that suggested, I think, to Lomax that he record Jelly talking about New Orleans history and the music. So that was in the spring of 1938 when Lomax first met him and he went out to the library.
And to your knowledge, that's the first taped interview, I guess you could say it was in a way, of any New Orleans musician. Or would that be fair to say, the first oral history you've done?

Possibly. Possibly that it was recorded, at least. As far as I know. It might have been something. It wasn't taped, of course, they didn't have tape until after the World War II in this country. But it was done as Lomax once mentioned to him, he was on a broken down Presto, he called it. Which, of course, unfortunately didn't run the right speed. It was running a little too slow, I guess it was, or something. Anyway, the pitch came out wrong. Which makes the thing too high, I guess, when you play it back at, say, 78. So, it's funny, in the Lomax book he talks about that nobody ever suspected the thing was going to run into, say, over a hundred sides. When he started, he thought it was going to be just, you know, a couple of sides, like his other blues people and gospel people that he recorded. But in an interview, which Jelly had in the paper, before he did those, I found the interview, it took me months almost to find it, weeks of, not that solid word, but before I ever did find it, in the Library of Congress. A Saturday night, I think it was one of the evening papers. More or less of a little tabloid, a small size paper. And in that paper, Jelly tells how he's going to go out to the library and make these records. Because he'd already contacted Lomax.

Jelly Roll in the Library of Congress. Anyway, to finish up the little article, the interview in the newspaper, it's funny, and Jelly outlines how this is going to be a big project. I think he may even mention it's going to take a hundred sides or so. And Lomax, of course, had no idea that Jelly had the whole thing already organized in his mind. And it wasn't that organized, I mean, but Lomax, of course, had to ask him the questions and lead him on from one subject to another and all these pieces. But at least Jelly did have in mind that it was going to be a big project. It wasn't only one or two records or one or two dates. It was going to run into a hundred records or so. So I don't know when I met Jelly. I didn't know anything about the Library of Congress sides at that time until maybe a year or so later. I'm not sure when I...
Did he then go up to New York again? Is that where you met him?

I met him first a couple of times, maybe three times in Washington. And then the last time I saw him was in New York in September of 1939. Or no, wait, 1940. A couple of months before he went to California. He died out there then six months later. But he did make those... I think the Library of Congress is mostly done in the month of May, probably. They don't have all the dates in the Lomax book, anything about it, exact dates usually. But I don't even know how many it was, but it ran on for several days.
Well, if I'm not mistaken, it was Jelly's music that first got you interested in jazz. And you collected, started collecting.

Actually, Jelly, yeah, this Jelly Roll record that I picked up at a little school. I was teaching a band, brass band, and some of the instrumental music out on Staten Island. The kids would have records they'd play during their lunch period. And after the school session, they left this one record there. I mean, they left a lot of records there, but I picked up this one record of Jelly Roll Martin and his Red Hot Peppers and the Shoeshiners Drag, it was. So I thought it was a funny title and a funny name of a band. I just wondered what on earth that could be. And I took it home and played it and liked it so well that I decided to try to get other Jelly's. I didn't know who was on the record. I didn't even know he was from New Orleans. At that time, Jelly was living up in Harlem. I was living up on Riverside Drive. It wasn't, it was in the worst section of it. Riverside Drive was sort of a millionaire's row at one time. This was up near 125th Street, where the, near the Sheffield Milk Factory was right in back of our place.
You could have met him, actually. Yeah, yeah. Quite easily.

Yeah, Jelly was living over on 131st Street, roughly. If not the 131st, some other street in there. He lived sometimes on the 131st Street. First at Joplin's house at one time, then later in the 38th he lived all the time there on the 138th, near 7th Avenue. So it would be the same section, which would have been, oh, a dozen blocks to go a little across town, and then up about six or seven blocks. And I could have seen Jelly and heard him play. He wasn't working much. That was the Depression already. So he wasn't working very much. But at least, oh, one of the first people I talked to, I was living down in the village on Bank Street. This was 1933, I believe, in New York. And there was a fellow, his name was Talbot, or something like that. Talbot or Talbot. He lived up in the attic. We both had attic rooms there in this Bank Street place. And he collected records, and he had several Jelly records, and some Louis Armstrong records, and Henderson records. And he had just graduated from high school a year or so before. And he mentioned for their senior prom they had Jelly Roll. And I didn't even know if Jelly was from New Orleans or what color he was. Of course, he was practically white when you look at him anyway. But I didn't know if he was New Orleans or anything about him until this fellow told me about him. I don't know. I think he knew he was from New Orleans. But he told about how the band, they had a big tuba player. He thought he was an Indian. He looked like an American Indian, at least part Indian, that played tuba. And how he would rock from side to side with the beat, you know, when he played. And he was trying to get all the Louis Armstrong. He wasn't a really systematic record collector. But I mean, he had quite a few Louis. Pick up any Louis that he'd see. Jelly's, too. So I already had a few Jelly records by that time. But I had no idea if he was from New Orleans or where he was. Whether he was in New York or...
How much of him had you collected before you actually met him? Had you on the complete record?

By the time I met him, I had probably three-fourths of his records. I remember when, just by way of introduction, I was just about as bad as Hullsizer, who used to play all the Jelly records for Jelly. You'd take him over to his house, Jelly, over to Hullsizer's house. Hullsizer was a record collector from Ohio and happened to be living in Washington about the 1938 period, too. And he'd play all of these records and ask Jelly who's on this record and, you know, tried to get personnel. Jelly couldn't remember some of them. He was confused. They'd been made, oh, 10 to 12 years before most of them. So Jelly wasn't really too interested, either. And so after an hour or so of that, he could tell Jelly was really fed up and he'd go over and look out of the window down at his car. So then Hullsizer said he knew it was time to quit. So I also began talking about records to Jelly and told him that I had a lot of the records and mentioned some of the titles. And I remember he seemed interested at that time that I had those. He went in back to the kitchen, a woman by the name of Mrs. Lyle had started this place called the Jungle Inn, it was called the Music Box when I went there in 1938. And he said, oh, here's the man that's got all of my records. He went back. Actually, he'd had a few of his records on the Jukebox even at that time. Or whatever you own.
Yeah, we're on the subject of critics.
Well, we own all that. Who was Gene Williams? And I never did quite know how he got in the picture and when and when. Was he in the book?

No, he's not. No, he was a student at Columbia University along with Ralph Gleason and a couple other people he knew like Barry Olenov is that his name, the one-time editor of Metronome and Tori Dano was another of his friends there. So I know Gleason's talked about how he started reviewing, Gleason began reviewing records for the Columbia College paper just so he could get free records, I guess, from the companies mostly. And Gene probably did some of that work too. Anyway, Gene started about as soon as he was out of college around 1939, the Jazz Information little paper. More like a mimeographed offset printing or something at first. It only ran about two years or so. But he got much interested in New Orleans music in particular. And he's the one that promoted the first Bunk recording. Only he wanted me to record Bunk in 1942. But the day before I was starting down here to do it, he got a letter from Dave Stewart that Dave was going to come over here and record Bunk. All that Dave had in mind was bring a little home recorder along and maybe record Bunk playing by himself in New Iberia or something. But anyway, Gene decided then to come down too. His health hadn't been very good. He thought he had TB once in a lung trouble. It wasn't really that serious, I don't think. But he came down here too, and then they decided that Dave would better do the recording issue because he had a lot of pressure on his label since he was able to get pressings. That was during the war, and you couldn't even get shellac pressings those days. But Dave at least had some contact and even sold 10,000 of one of his Lou Waters records. So it was through his magazine and all that Gene became known, you might say. And then he had inherited a little money, not very much. In those days, if you inherited $10,000 or so, it was a big amount, everybody thought. But he did decide to promote Bunk's band in New York in 1945 when they went to the Stuyvesant Casino. And then he later went to San Francisco about a year or two later, and had Ori's band to play at a place out there called the Green Room.
Speaking about Bunk Johnson, how many people were involved really in his coming back? Was there quite a group of people interested in him? I know you played a large part.
No, actually not so many people were there again. There was only a handful of people.
Uh-huh.

That seemed interested in trying to even want to hear him. The early Jazzmen records were so badly recorded and distributed too that they only sold a few hundred, I guess, of each of those probably. And Bunk did attract an awful lot of attention when he got to New York. Oh, a dozen national magazines, everything from Pick and Life. I don't know if it was Life. I don't know if Life had him. Other papers, though, they all had stories on him.
Call you.
Call you.
How do you explain this interest in him?
Well, anybody that heard the band, it was something new. They'd never heard anything quite like that, up in New York especially. And the band really did go.
Uh-huh.

I was talking to people the other night, somebody over at Preservation Hall played a tune twice. I was surprised. I don't know if that was Alvin Alcorn, who it was Willie Humphrey, who's a band, I guess it was, did it. And I was just thinking, that Bunk band in New York, they'd hardly ever played a piece once, and usually more than twice, quite often three or four times, people would like, they'd keep clapping, and that's when the Saints became popular, even more than Louie's record, which had been on jukeboxes in a very limited extent, limited extent in the 30s, late 30s, 38, about 39. But somehow the record never did really go in place. The jazz, other jazz bands, never did take up the tune and play it. But after Bunk played it, everybody, I'd say more than anybody, Bunk's the one that is responsible for the Saints being such a nuisance as it is today, even the football team being named there. But, and that was due to people in person hearing the band more than anything, because his records weren't that good or weren't sold that many. Even the Victor and the Decca didn't sell very many, I would say. But there again, it was still a handful of people, actually, but Bunk could have, with the right kind of breaks and all and circumstances, he could have really gone places too. I mean, if he'd gotten, say, on radio and made some good records, you only have to really make about one good record, it's only... Most people make a hit record, I mean, it starts selling by the millions or by maybe a million. You don't need a dozen hit records. Like I say, begin the beginning, one of Artie Shaw, for instance. It was a big hit, and after that, well, his name is made and it sweeps the country. Same way with Benny Goodman. I don't remember now what his first big hit was. But if Bunk had happened to make one good record of some kind...
Did you ever hear King Port of Stomp by Goodman?
Yeah, I don't know that that was the one that did it, though.
Sometimes I'm happy. They were back to back.
Yeah.
Let's Dance, of course, is the same.
Maybe the Let's Dance, I'm sure. Let's Dance, that's what I was thinking of.
Yeah.
Well... Same way with Glenn Miller, in the mood, one of his was either like Moonlight or Sunrise Serenade, I believe is the one that did it for him.
Well, what were the circumstances that didn't allow him to do that?

Well, the band didn't get along, and if they had stayed there and had been able to maybe get some radio engagements, which they did have a few chances, and even people in movies talking would come there, you see. If something like that had happened, why, the thing could have gone on to... Because it certainly got enough publicity in national magazines, in New York magazines that were centered around there, you might say.

How did they see him? Did they see him as a proponent of the... I mean, as a representative of the pure New Orleans style? Did they even know that that existed? Well, ordinarily, the people that would go in there just to dance wouldn't even know or care too much. But the press, I mean, how would they talk about him?

Yeah, they played up the New Orleans angle a good deal, and the fact that his age and all, he wasn't really that old. He died before he was 70. And when you say, look at some place like Preservation Hall, people that are going there in their 70s, Jim Robinson at 85 now, as good as he ever was, practically, maybe not quite as much lung power or powerful, and he can't dance quite like he used to, but he gets along all right at 85. He may only be 83, actually.
Or he may be 93. No, I don't think he's 93, but I mean, you know.
And Chink Martin goes pretty good. He usually takes it very easy, but the other night when he played with a good band for a change, and he really played. I was surprised.
If they ever got a good band over there, I wish you'd let me know.
Sound like Chester's Arbs on this.
Chester's artist is very good. He usually gets a real arousing...
Usually Chink, you know, looks like he's half asleep over there leaning against the wall.
What does Chink Martin play the drums?
The string bass. Oh, the string bass. I haven't seen him over there. He was on the first records, I guess, the Jelly ever made.
Do you know?
Back in 1922 or so.
Saturday, I enjoyed Paul Bond's playing the most that I can remember.
Oh, up at...
Up at 290.
Was he really good? I wondered what happened. We don't take up the tape. I'd like to hear about it.
I'll tell you about it later. I just think it's remarkable that I... You know, how long have I been listening? I'm talking about on clarinet, not on sax. But, I mean, he only played clarinet.
Actually, that soprano sax, that's what we did on Deep Creek. The Deep Creek, as it should be called.

Any case, it was my favorite, you know, live performance on clarinet that I've ever heard and he seemed to play a much older style, which can happen occasionally with New Orleans musicians. I mean, he's not like Mealy who could sort of change styles. It will, according to the trumpet play he was playing with, the band he was with.
He really went back. He can play all rights. Other times, it's sort of cut and dried and not too good a tone sometimes today.
This was not a legit clarinet tone. We was playing ratty clarinet. That's what I'm trying to say.
With a small group, was it?
Yeah, Nelson, Dolio, and Sales on guitar. Go ahead.
Do you have any other questions there?

Well, yeah, just with, I know that you recorded Bunk Johnson's band on your own record label. And I wanted to just ask you a little bit about how the American Records Company, I think was the name of your...
Yeah, just call it American Music.
American Music got started and how that relates to Bunk Johnson being well known. Or did that help his cause? Yeah, we might talk a little about that.

The reason I got into the business at all was partly due to these first records I mentioned, the Jazzmen, that were so badly recorded on the little machine. About a $200 list price machine it was, a federal recorder. Some kid that worked, he was a teenage kid, I guess, that worked for Grunewald's. Happened to have it. He's the only one we could find that had any blanks around that would be able to record the band in 1942 when Dave issued the records. And those records were so bad that I'll tell you one story that I'll illustrate it. Dave wanted to stop, take his time. He was driving back to California, so he packed up the masters about a dozen sides or so. On steel, they were steel base, I guess. They weren't glass. He wouldn't have shipped them. They were steel base acetates. And I think it was Allied recording, the biggest factory out there. They had a studio, too, in Los Angeles. And they'd been pressing the Lou Waters records for him. So he sent these masters on to his friend, who was the engineer, somebody there, and told him to start work on them so he'd be ready to issue them, you know, when he got back or something. So he got back maybe a week or maybe almost two weeks later. And so he goes there to the studio to get the records and see what work's been done. And the guy started laughing. He said, Oh, he said, you really meant that? He thought it was a joke. He thought they sent him those things just as a horrible example, you know, of how bad recording could be. And... ... ...

He hadn't thrown them out fortunately, but he probably would have very soon if Dave hadn't gotten back. He could have thrown them in a wastebasket. So he thought it was just a joke, you know, that he sent something to amuse him. So Dave said, no, that's the real thing. It had to be worked on and issued. So anyway, I decided after that that I couldn't do much worse. So I got a machine. My machine only cost about $40. My brother put a little secondhand machine together and then bought an amplifier. My brother was a good electrical engineer in Pittsburgh where I was living during the war. So the first year I recorded the George Lewis climax records. And if anything, they did come out, I guess, the worst recording in a lot of ways. As you can tell from some of them, the bad starts that we get and some of them had to fade out. I had so much trouble with the needle, the cutting needle, sort of bouncing, jumping along due to some kind of a vibration. It's very peculiar. I still have some of those masters. Unbelievable looks when you look at the records. So my guess that I couldn't do any worse was almost wrong there. But the music came out pretty good on its climax. I sold them to Blue Note. Put them on a non-union climax label, it was. Because none of the guys at that time belonged to the union. Except the funny thing is, there was supposed to be a pianist on there, Walter Deku. They'd been on the Bunk records. This was 1943, I'm talking about now. And I came down here. First, I was supposed to record Bunk that year. I'd been writing to him about recording. Then about a week before I came down here, I was working for the same transformer company. My brother was out. He was the chief engineer, and I was just working in the test department. So the whole factory would close down for one week, and everybody had to take their vacation at that time. So anyway, a week before I was due for my vacation to come down here and record, my Bunk suddenly went to San Francisco. That's when he went out there. Rudy Blasher had a concert called This Is Jazz. And he'd appeared at the museum. He later played weekly sessions there, called the CIO Room. Well anyway, I went out then to San Francisco to hear that concert, because they had Ori's band to come up from California with Mud Carry. And others to play with Bunk. So I did record Bunk playing informally with Bertha Gonsolin, a pianist. A lady who'd come from New Orleans. She'd been out there. She'd even played a few dates with Oliver in 1922 or so, when Oliver was out there. So then I came on to San Francisco, I came on to New Orleans and recorded George Lewis then, which I'd hoped would be something that fit the issue commercially. Recording-wise, it was pretty bad, but the music was very good. It was George's first session under his own name, and they were really going good that day. With Kid Howard, his lip was in good shape, and Jim and all played well. But we were supposed to have a pianist, the same pianist that played with Bunk the year before, Walter Deku. And unfortunately, he was a member of the union. We did this over at a place called the Gypsy Tea Room. It had been called the Japanese Tea Room until we got in the war, and they had to change the name real quick. So a great big nightclub room. In front of it was a bar, a little room in front of the bar. And it turned out the union, I don't know what it would be called, the Board of Trustees or Executive Board or something of the union, was having their weekly or... At that time, they had both white and colored unions. And they were having their weekly meeting there in the... One corner of this big nightclub hall. So I guess Walter Deku came to the door and saw the union executives back there in the corner, so he never came in for the date. Which we didn't really miss the piano anyway, because most of the guys were used to playing without piano. In fact, George hadn't used the piano hardly ever in any of his jobs. Because the small clubs here, if they have a piano, if half of the keys will sound, they're all out of tune anyway, or too low when they can't tune up to it. And of course on parades, and they'd advertise on wagons, which they still did somewhat in those days, in the 40s even, why they'd be on trucks, of course. They didn't use piano. So all of the guys here always have been used and still are able to play without piano. So we didn't really miss the piano. But that's why there is no piano on there. So anyway, the next year I got another recording machine. It was also in pretty bad shape. I got it only one day before it came down here. We bought it secondhand for about, I don't remember the price, say $150 or something. And the turntable wouldn't even move. It was just sort of rusted, corroded into the thing. But my brother got it out some way and used emery paper and got it working very smoothly. And it worked very good mechanically, except it was the wrong speed. Everything was recorded at 81.6 in place of 78. And so everything came out sounding about a half a tone too low. If you play it back at 78, then you're playing it too slow. A lot of the records I issued had to be issued that way because when I'd have them mastered at some of the studios, New York, different places, where they could only play one speed if they had a, say, asynchronous motor that went according to how many cycles the current was going. So anyway, some of the recording of that wasn't too bad. But there again, I didn't know how to use the machine. I had a lot of trouble for thread even that second year. And I know Hugh Davis, who was the engineer that mastered most of those early bunk sides, complained bitterly that there were no highs at all. He said there was, I mean, no lows at all. Practically nothing below middle C, he said, on the thing. Of course, he was expecting, he'd been used to recording big bands like the Ellington Band and things. And it had a big bass section with maybe a couple of basses and piano and baritone, saxes and everything else. But let's see, all we had was the trombone, which a lot of times doesn't hardly go below middle C anyway. And the string bass, which unfortunately didn't pick up too well. But it wasn't a real heavy sounding bass anyway. But some of that recording wasn't too bad with that machine, actually. The next year I had the speed adjusted so that we could record a 78. But it was a pretty bad recording, actually, anybody would have to admit. Although I remember some of the numbers we did the next year, though, when Ewing Nunn, who's probably the most, I don't know what you'd say, the most engineer of anybody I know, a wonderful engineer. He's the son of the, he's still living, he's gone out of the business now. But he'd done probably the best recording I ever heard, as far as, he had the audiophile label. And he worked mostly in tape. He never did, he did have a disc machine at times he would use, though. But some of his recording was so good, I remember once I went into the studio once and I thought, surely there was a band playing in there, it turned out a tape machine. He would only record at 30 inches per minute, or per second, I mean, 30 inch speed, in place of 15 or like most of these machines.
This is the fourth, okay, I got the fourth reel on.

Talking about the American Music Records, I started to say that Nunn said some of the recording wasn't too bad. None? He said that's as good as they do at Victor. Of course, he thought, he called Victor engineers a bunch of schoolboys, which they were compared to Nunn.
But you mean like John Reed?

No, John never worked in the record department. He met some of the engineers, that would be in the 1950s. But anyway, recording is nothing to brag about. But I decided then to issue some of the things myself. In 1945, I decided to go into the business myself and issue them. So I began getting impressed. That was during the war wasn't over yet, even. But we couldn't even get the pressings, except from the, what's it called, Muzak? Is that the name of the company that pipes music, you know, into the different factories and hotels and everything else?
That's music.

They could get pressings, vinyl pressings, 12-inch pressings only. So that's what I issued my stuff on, this red transparent or translucent vinyl for about a year or so. But some of those might have sold as many as a thousand. Most of them would sell maybe 300 or 600. Usually have them pressed in 300 lots, I believe it was. So the records never could have been that important in influencing or promoting the music. But at least a few of the jazz fanatics, you might say, and record collectors heard of Bunk. Threw this through your records. Yeah, but the records weren't that good that they could put him over as a competitor of, say, Artie Shaw or Glenn Miller. Oh, well. Benny Goodman and those people. Who was your public relations man?
But wasn't, I mean, would you say you recorded quite a bit of the total that was recorded of him?

Oh, possibly. A lot of other people recorded him. But maybe in total number of sides. Of course, now they've been reissuing, or not only reissuing, but also issuing some new material in Japan. Second masters and rejects and all, I would have called them. Some of those rejects aren't any worse than the first ones, really. And some of them are actually pretty good at times. And there's hardly an excuse to issue four or five masters of one tune, like, say, Sister Kate. But let's see, the last Sister Kate, though, that they mastered, which was a year ago or two years ago, I forget now, turned out to be one of the best ones. It was really quite terrific, I thought, to hear it on, you know, when you play the original master, which we did at the studio, you hear that original master, which hadn't been played maybe more than once. So it was really good, fresh cut there. And there aren't people around like Bunk anymore. I mean, I remember the breaks there, and some of the breaks the whole band would take, one of them. They were really some terrific music on that.
There wasn't any soloing as such then. Was there a soloing of instruments? It was all purely on sound.

There was, when Bunk was feeling good, he wouldn't ever put his horn down. In fact, that was the tradition in New Orleans. There might be sometimes, say, at times maybe the clarinet could have been a leader of a band, and he might have sort of featured himself at times. But ordinarily, the trumpet should never put his horn down at all. And that should go for a brass band, too, out on the street. Some of the guys in the old days would, like Wooden Joe, I know. I've seen him play, and heard him play a whole parade when he'd be the only trumpet. So he couldn't put, nowadays not only do they take rests, they have usually now three trumpets, as they say, so you can have two up and one down. I used to think that meant two playing up high and one down low. But what they mean is one down resting. But today the bands, the trumpet section, the whole section will put their horns down, and they'll have a trombone solo or a sax solo.
Is that how the solo got started? Well, I don't know.

I don't know where they really started. I always consider the best example. I use an expression of Eddie Condon jam sessions. Especially these big town hall sessions. They used to have maybe sometimes three or four small bands. And the final numbers they'd all get on the stage at one time, they'd all have to take a solo, you know, each one of them. About a dozen to twenty solos strung out in a row. And maybe one ensemble chorus to start and one ensemble chorus to end. And unfortunately that's the way a lot of the bands play today in New Orleans and all over, of course. Which means there's very little ensemble playing. Although they can still do it. And you can't blame them if they want to take things easy sometime. And of course if there's a lot of tourists coming here to hear bands, why they expect to hear solos.
I was going to ask you how the tourist audience affects the jazz style here. Like a place like Reservation Hall.

It might affect it to some degree because the people know what the audience expects. And maybe even likes in some cases to see somebody. It isn't a question of exactly showing off and all. A lot of times it's just a question of taking it easy, you know. No need to kill themselves playing. Although Bunk never had that attitude. I point out in one of the notes one time where somebody after a dance asked Bunk, if he wasn't awfully tired. He looked at him and he couldn't believe it.

How can you get tired playing music? And playing is playing. It's not working. It's having a good time. In the same way in a parade. I mean, when you go to a parade to follow it along, you don't know until the whole parade's over that you're tired, that you've maybe been walking for several miles and all.
Well, didn't the unionization cause a lot of this regimentation of taking certain breaks every half hour? Did that contribute to it?

Yeah, but not necessarily. Sometimes, maybe before the union, they might have even taken longer breaks at times. I mean, it depends on what would go on. I mean, but on the other hand, they were used to longer hours. I mean, they might start at 8 o'clock in the evening and play until 4 o'clock in the morning, even. And as far as long hours going, when you hear about these taxi dance halls, where they, you know, a dime a dance or a nickel a dance, they might have been in the old days, where they can hardly put their instruments down. They just have a few seconds there. And sometimes that would go on for several hours, almost without stopping. And in order to get a little rest or lunch, some of the guys would double on one instrument, on another instrument. Maybe, say, if they had a pianist, one of the horns might play on the piano for a while so the pianist could take a rest and eat a sandwich and so on. But those were probably some of the toughest jobs you hear about because they could hardly stop at all. There again, they would probably play as easy as they could, maybe taking solos there too to get rest.
You would remember more clearly than I, but for example, at Speck's Moulin Rouge, I remember Kid Thomas would take a break, eat a sandwich. Now, what time was that?
Oh, I don't know.
Seems to me it was about midnight.

Yeah, it would be pretty late. I was going to say at least by 11 o'clock, they might start early too. They didn't play so late. They didn't go until maybe after 1 or 2 o'clock either, did they? I don't think.
I don't know because my memories after midnight get very, very fuzzy there.

Yeah. But anyway, as I say, sometimes they would find excuses for whether there was a union or not to take breaks at times. And in some clubs that they'd play in, sometimes the owner doesn't want the band to play all the time because when people are dancing or listening to music or whatever they're doing, they're not drinking, you know. So sometimes they want them to take long breaks. I've been in clubs and situations where they, I've noticed those things too, where the owner would want them to take a long break so they'd sell more drinks in between. But it's not an unreasonable rule of the union, I think about 15 minutes for every hour or so, that they deserve a break. But...
So that's not a contributing factor to what you're talking about.

No, I don't think that's contributing to this. What? Stop it. I mean, Bunk never considered it hard work that he'd have to be playing all the time. Sometime maybe when his lip wasn't always in shape, he didn't play all the time. Sometime he'd stop and light a cigarette in the middle. Some of the, even the record sessions, he sort of drops out in the middle of a chorus and people think, well, his lip got tired, he's an old man, he was 60 years old or something, and just worn out. And so he had to stop. But maybe what he did was stop and light a cigarette, you know, put his horn down for a minute and then pick it up whenever he wanted to. But if he were really feeling good and had confidence in all the players and knew that they all knew the tune and the way they were supposed to play it, well, he would be playing a second part and be filling in when some of the others were, taking solos, whatever you'd want to call them. But some of the records I made weren't that way all the way through. Occasionally he'd play all the way through a number, but usually he'd take off and let George Lewis take a chorus or so. But Jim would never stop, usually. And Jim, even today, complains bitterly when the trumpet puts his horn down quite often. Some certain players he'll refuse to play with regularly, say even at Preservation Hall, because they're too lazy, as he would say.
They don't play the lead? No, they just want to sit there and rest. Oh, I see. And Jim said, that's no way to do.

I came across the old notes I'd taken once over at Preservation Hall about five or six years ago, or maybe ten years ago, I think they were. I happened to be sitting out in the carriageway there on those benches, and Jim was there. He wasn't playing that night. And so I copied down the remarks he was making after he left. I didn't copy them down, but mostly word for word. And he would say, what kind of a band, what kind of a trumpet player? Where's the trumpet player? He'd keep saying, where's the trumpet player? Don't hear the trumpet player. You know, he couldn't see in there. He knew that he wasn't playing. He was just ridiculing him. And he'd say, that's no way to have a band. That's no way for a trumpet player to do to put his horn down at all, you see. So in some cases, you might think that would add more monotony to the music, you know, everything the same. But another thing they did in the old days, which Jelly talks about a lot, the triple 40 bands, as Jelly calls them, that they should, you know, this business of the glass of water. He goes into that on one of the Library of Congress, where if you have a glass of water half full, you can add to it and take away and all. In the old days, they had these routines Bunkies talked about and Baby Dodds used to talk about it too. Most of the New Orleans bands would follow. It was almost a convention, you might say, a tradition to do it that way, that you hit the introduction loud, as they say, the forte, and then maybe they'd drop down just a little bit, but still with the full tone for the first few choruses, and then they'd drop down quite soft, maybe come up a little bit, and right before the end, they'd drop down so soft that you could hardly hear it. There was somebody who was, when I was down in Bermuda a month ago, must have been Willie Humphrey or Percy or somebody talking about, too, how some of the dances they used to play, they'd play so soft too, that you couldn't, they couldn't hear themselves play, and that next to the last chorus or so.
I think it was King Oliver who said that he wanted his band to be able to play so soft they could hear the dancers shuffling.

Yeah, I think that's quoted in Jasmine as a Bolden remark, whether it was, yeah, it was supposed to be a Bolden remark. They say, way down, way down low, so I can hear those whores drag their feet on the floor. I don't know who told me that, Richard M. Jones or somebody, that they'd heard Bolden say that. I don't know whether it's strictly true, but anyway, that was very much the New Orleans tradition. The Ori band followed that.
What was that? Was that for the, part of the form of it, the definite form, or did it build momentum towards the end, or?

Well, yeah, just to give more contrast, and then to make the final all-out chorus, as they called it, more effective. More effective, yeah. I know once, I used to question Minnetta, since he played violin, whether you could really hear the violin in the band, because you'd wonder, you know, since I try to play violin myself, in, say, a ragtime band, and half the time you can't hear it unless there's a microphone and amplifier there, and Minnetta said, too, you could hardly hear the violin most of the time. Maybe sometime, the only time you'd hear it would be that very soft chorus before the end. That's maybe also the only time you'd really hear the guitar come out good, too, because they used guitar in the old-time bands rather than the banjo before, say, the 1920s. The banjo.
They hear Sales on Saturday.
Came back.
Sales is loud. I was really surprised that I lied to you.
Ordinarily, Sales isn't real loud, like, say, as loud as Gayno, or...
I'm talking about guitar.
Yeah, oh, on guitar.
Yeah, I mean, he was playing with Milford Dahlio, who's not a soft drummer.
I would never think of him, but... It was an electric, but Gale has an electric guitar, too. He has used it.
No, I think he got rid of his electric.
Yeah, I mean, years ago.
Years ago, yeah, but I think he got rid of all that stuff. He's gone back to acoustic in his product.
Yeah.
And I thought that was very interesting to hear, you know, cutting through the way he did, and you can hear the fullness of his sound on guitar.

Yeah, the Ori band always used it. Of course, Bud Scott, in the days I heard him, he always played guitar, too. He could play banjo, might have done it on a few special numbers sometime, but almost always just guitar. And the Ori band also softened down a lot at times. I mean, they had a lot of variety and dynamics, you might say. What I feel is that there always is a tradition going on, and you're very aware of the novelty things that come out, and the tradition just keeps on going and people come back to it. And it may die out very gradually, but, you know, we keep looking. Look at all the different things that have happened, all the many revivals that have come back. It's really, it's been a relatively short time that New Orleans jazz died out.
Yeah.

I mean, look at, well, 1940, I was thinking about Louis and Bechet getting together in that band. Bro on bass, you know, where they made the Colcord Blues and done it. Wanky Dock Town and all those things.

By the way, when they, they had an Esquire program, they had an all-star band, you know, Esquire. And so they gave some of the awards down here. I think it was a three-way hookup they had. Benny Goodman was in New York, somebody in San Francisco, and Louis, I believe, in New Orleans. The three of them or so got together. Well, anyway, they played one piece over earphones. But they also gave a concert here at the auditorium. They had George Lewis's band. Bunk was there, too. Is that the night they changed the name? I guess they changed the name back to Basin Street from Saratoga. I always remember Leonard Feather talking about who didn't like Bunk at all and never really heard him, I guess, in person, probably. But it was always ridiculing because he would miss a note maybe here and there sometime with his lip. Anyway, he told about when Bunk and Louis played Basin Street together, that Louis, it was a good solo that Louis took, and Bunk breathing heavily in the background or something. Actually, it was Louis. I mean, Bunk was taking the solo part. Feather thought it was Louis. But anyway, the point I was going to make, Sidney Bechet came down for the concert, too, and played with his own group, I think, with James P. Johnson, Higginbottom, the others were there. And they got together with Louis on one number or so. At the rehearsal, George Lewis and some of them told me about that Bechet and Louis didn't get along at all. That Bechet was trying to play the lead, of course, the soprano sax is almost in a trumpet range and more of a trumpet-like instrument anyway than the clarinet in a way. So, at least the way Sidney used it, usually as the leader of his own band, always to play the lead. And Louis, you know, he got really red hot and said, I ain't going to have no two leads in my band. And I don't know if he was trying to get Sidney either to play his clarinet or play a different variation part on it. So, they could, though, if any time Sidney wanted to, he could still play a good clarinet part, and he did occasionally in bands. But he and Bunk didn't get along when they went to Boston either, and that was another reason there, too. Sidney told him he was going to go back and play clarinet with the group. And, as Bunk said, I didn't come up here to play no Dixieland band, and especially no Race Horse Dixieland. And Sidney would stop those things off so fast that Bunk couldn't even keep up with him. But still, Sidney could if he wanted to. He had enough. He was an exceptional talent, naturally. But when he got away from New Orleans, too, he changed his style quite a bit. I wonder if I ought to answer that bell. You want me to go get it? Can you turn it off for a minute, maybe? Well, I'll go get it. All right, we can turn it off.
And tell him you've only got about two or three minutes. Yeah.

We'll swine this tape. There's another five minutes on there. Yeah, I'll tell him. Come back in five minutes. Maybe somebody just wants to get in somebody else's apartment. Let's see. What, we were talking about New Orleans style. How it's been generated.

Yeah, and how it changed to the solo style. And I thought I had entertained the idea once that the people that developed the solo style might not have fit in socially with the kind of communal ensemble.
I don't know, because I think Louis could go back at times and play in a simple style. Maybe a few times did on certain records and certain dates.

One of the interesting things about Louis that I think is very significant for the idea of him as a performer is that he never considered himself a musician. He considered himself an entertainer. That he was in a tradition of, well, that there was no separation between pleasing people and being an entertainer and the music. And if I'm correct, in a sense the New Orleans style, or New Orleans music, is so much a part of the social surroundings that it's more than music. It's the whole context.
Yeah, I would expect it's a way of life of always working together.
Yeah, a way of life.
That would have to do with a lot of other things in their life, too, the way they had to work together in order to survive, you might say.

And the trouble with this is that a lot of critics will come back on that and say, well, Louis was an entertainer, he wasn't a musician. But I think that if one understands the New Orleans tradition, those two things were very close.

Yeah, the entertaining is a part of it. I know a friend of mine, Bill Colburn, who lived with Bunk quite a while, a lot longer than I did, would explain that Bunk would play anything for anybody if he knew the tune at all, and also try to play in a way that people like. It was Louis Prima, his motto, did the poor guy ever recover?
Well, he's in a convalescent home here now.
Did he ever become conscious? He was in a coma last time.
No, I don't know whether he's conscious. Well, anyway, Louis Prima. Today, I think, on the radio.

Yeah. His motto, the slogan was, play pretty for the people. They used to even print that, you know, along with his name and all. But that was the motto of all the New Orleans people. They were trying to play. Ori made a big point of that, too, trying to play sweet and as pretty as you can for the people, not as rough and loud.
Wouldn't that depend on where they were playing, though?

Yeah, that's it. But if I should say in a dance hall where they should play just good dance music, and not, there again, maybe unjustly, I use as an example the Eddie Condon bunch, say the bunch of Knicks, or say Jazz Limited in Chicago, where if you request something that isn't the so-called Dixieland number, well, they'll be insulted, you know, if you'd ask them to play some late popular tune. Well, no, that's not one of our numbers. In other words, they consider themselves as artists, and they're playing in some ways for themselves. They're playing these New Orleans classics or Dixieland classics. But the New Orleans people themselves, they would play anything. The latest popular tune or the latest, or any of the oldest folk songs or anything. Like Bunk always, some of his biggest numbers were bell-bottom trousers in New York. And they all laugh about him. In California, he wanted to play Marezy Dotes with some of the Louvoters. Well, Louvot wasn't even there, so we shouldn't drag in his name as blaming him. But some of the other guys, they just refused to play a tune like Marezy Dotes. And yet Bunk, he was hurt because he wanted to play anything like that. People would request those tunes, and he wants to play them for the people. So, just as Bill Colburn explained, if you go in a restaurant and order, say, beef steak, and the guy said, oh no, I'm sorry, you're going to have pork chops. I'm the cook today. I'm the waiter. I'm the pork professional. No, don't insult us. We're going to give you what we want. We know what's good for you. And they said, I would like to have this well done. Oh no, you're not going to have a well done steak. You're going to get this rare. That's the way to cook it. And that's the way, you might say, some of the later jazz musicians, as I say unjustly, I blame it just to say the Eddie Conlon group in some respects were that way. And the jazz limited too. They'd refuse to play any requests. It wasn't strictly something that they thought was a classic. But Bunk would play any old tune, whether it's Maresy Dotes or Bell Bottom Trousers. And they always were that way.
It seems to me that the New Orleans style music depended very importantly on having a certain mood, that one had to be in a good mood. You couldn't decide to say, forget it.

Yeah, that's right. Baby Dodds makes a big point of that. And that wasn't part of a chapter in that book about how it's to make people happy. Well, Bunk always stressed that too. Music's to make people happy. They're paid entertainers, just like a cook or anybody else. Go in a restaurant, you pay the cook to give you what you want. Was it Shakespeare or something? He said he who pays the pipe or calls the tune or somebody.
Something like that.
So we're running.

segments.title: Opening and Russell's pen name
segments.summary: Perhonas introduces the session at Russell's New Orleans home with Dick Allen. Russell explains he dropped his first name Wagner and wrote under William Russell from about 1930.

segments.title: First jazz records: Jelly Roll's Shoeshiners Drag and cheap Paramounts
segments.summary: Russell recalls hearing boat music as a child, then discovering jazz records in New York around 1928-29, starting with Jelly Roll Morton and buying Paramounts for three cents at Bloomfield's.

segments.title: John Hammond, early collectors and the Hot Record Exchange
segments.summary: Talk of Hammond as one of the earliest collectors, Fred Ramsey, and Steve Smith's Hot Record Exchange founded in 1936.

segments.title: Living in New York and hunting records on tour with a Chinese shadow play
segments.summary: Russell went to New York in 1929 to study violin and toured for years with a Chinese shadow play company, searching junk stores for hot jazz records and trying to find Louis Armstrong on Henderson sides.

segments.title: Early discographies and the first jazz books
segments.summary: Russell lists the first discographies and books on jazz, and says Jazzmen was the first to give New Orleans a section.

segments.title: First trips to New Orleans in the 1930s
segments.summary: Russell's brief early visits, a record-hunting trip with Park Breck, and hearing Tom Brown with Raymond Burke at the Dandy Inn.

segments.title: Researching and writing the New Orleans, Oliver and Armstrong chapters of Jazzmen
segments.summary: How Russell, Steve Smith and Lee Smith split the research, advances of about $30 each, Russell's Chicago interviews for the King Oliver chapter and his writing of the Armstrong chapter.

segments.title: Interviewing Louis Armstrong in New York
segments.summary: Russell interviews Armstrong near the Apollo and backstage at the Strand, plays him Ida Cox records, gets the new Decca catalog from Alpha, and asks about Bunk Johnson.

segments.title: The New Orleans revival: Nick's, Lu Watters and Jelly in New York
segments.summary: Russell argues the so-called revival was not really one, covering New Orleans players at Nick's, Jelly's 1938-40 New York stay, Lu Watters in California, and whether Jazzmen helped.

segments.title: Hugues Panassie's 1938 visit and his heroes
segments.summary: Russell recalls Panassie's trip to New York, his refusal to go to Chicago, his admiration for Mezzrow and Fats Waller, and his money.

segments.title: Eddie Condon's role among the musicians
segments.summary: Discussion of Condon as organizer, wit and non-virtuoso guitarist who hired New Orleans players at his club.

segments.title: Panassie's Victor sessions and Jelly's 1939 Victor date tied to Jazzmen
segments.summary: Panassie's favorites, his Victor sessions with Bechet and Ladnier, and how Steve Smith tied Jelly's Victor session to the Jazzmen publication.

segments.title: Jelly Roll Morton's Library of Congress recordings and Russell meeting him
segments.summary: Jelly's 1938 Lomax recordings, how he was discovered in Washington, the planned hundred sides, and Russell's meetings with him in Washington and New York.

segments.title: Finding Jelly's record and how close Russell lived to him in Harlem
segments.summary: Russell found the Red Hot Peppers record while teaching on Staten Island, and a Bank Street neighbor told him of Jelly's prom band.

segments.title: Playing records for Jelly, and interviewing Willie the Lion Smith
segments.summary: In one long block Russell recounts Hullsizer quizzing Jelly about records, Jelly preferring to play his new songs, and later paying Willie the Lion for an interview.

segments.title: Willie the Lion and the origins theories of jazz
segments.summary: Why Willie was not in Jazzmen, and the joke that he put jazz's birth in a brickyard in Newburgh or Haverstraw.

segments.title: John Hammond and the Bessie Smith chapter that never came
segments.summary: Hammond was to write the Bessie Smith chapter, the TV special on his life, and the afternoon Russell spent in his Columbia office.

segments.title: Whether Columbia kept Bessie Smith masters
segments.summary: Speculation on surviving Columbia masters, the company's many owners and how Brunswick and Decca rights confused reissues.

segments.title: The four editors and how Jazzmen was put together
segments.summary: Who edited Jazzmen, the contract, why only Ramsey's name went on the cover, and who gathered photographs.

segments.title: Fred Ramsey and how the chapters were assigned
segments.summary: Ramsey's job at Harcourt and tastes, and why Russell was asked to write on boogie woogie, Armstrong and New Orleans.

segments.title: Errors left in Jazzmen: 'Flee as a Bird' and later editions
segments.summary: The misprint 'Free as a Bird' that cost fifty cents a word to fix, and the book's copyright and armed-forces paperback.

segments.title: Royalties, complimentary copies and the price of books
segments.summary: Russell's Jelly Roll book, the copies owed to interviewees, and the cost of the Condon book.

segments.title: Wilton Crawley stories
segments.summary: Allen's Barberin story and Russell's anecdote about Wilton Crawley mistaken for an asylum patient, followed by a reel change.

segments.title: Otis Ferguson and Edward Nichols in Jazzmen
segments.summary: Perhonas asks about Ferguson's New Republic pieces on Bix and who wrote the Bix chapter.

segments.title: Roger Pryor Dodge and early jazz criticism
segments.summary: The chapter 'Consider the Critics', Charles Edward Smith's early writing, and Dodge's earlier articles.

segments.title: Dodge's film of Bunk and his friendship with Bubber Miley
segments.summary: Dodge as a ballet dancer, his silent movie of Bunk, and his friendship with Bubber Miley.

segments.title: E. Sims Campbell and why black writers wrote little on jazz
segments.summary: Question of black critics, Preston Jackson's articles, and George Gaynor's writing.

segments.title: Gene Williams and Jazz Information
segments.summary: Gene Williams's Jazz Information, his role in recording Bunk in 1942 and promoting Bunk's New York engagement in 1945.

segments.chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
segments.title: Bunk Johnson's New York engagement and why it never became a hit
segments.summary: Why so few people backed Bunk's return, the attention the band drew, 'The Saints', and what might have made Bunk a star.

segments.chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
segments.title: The press, Preservation Hall veterans and a clarinet performance
segments.summary: How the press played up Bunk's age, plus talk of Jim Robinson, Chink Martin and a Saturday clarinet set.

segments.chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
segments.title: Starting American Music: the Jazzmen records made on a toy machine
segments.summary: Perhonas asks how American Music began, and Russell begins with the badly recorded 1942 Bunk sides that Dave Stewart issued.

segments.chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
segments.title: Russell's own wartime recordings of Bunk and George Lewis
segments.summary: One long block on his cheap machines, the 1943 and 1944 sessions, the missing pianist at the Gypsy Tea Room, wrong speeds, and Ewing Nunn.

segments.chapter: Bunk Johnson and American Music records
segments.title: Pressing and selling American Music records
segments.summary: Nunn's praise, wartime vinyl pressings, small runs, how little they did to promote Bunk and the Japanese reissues.

segments.title: Solos, tourist audiences and Bunk's attitude to playing
segments.summary: Why a trumpeter never put his horn down, how solos spread, how tourists shape the music, and Bunk's view that playing is not work.

segments.title: Union breaks, long hours and taxi dance halls
segments.summary: Whether the union caused regimented breaks, with Allen recalling Kid Thomas at Speck's Moulin Rouge.

segments.title: Bunk, the cigarette and Jim Robinson on lazy trumpeters
segments.summary: Bunk put his horn down on purpose, and Jim Robinson complains of trumpeters who rest.

segments.title: Playing soft: dynamics in the old New Orleans bands
segments.summary: The triple-forte tradition Jelly described, Bolden's remark about hearing dancers drag their feet, and the quiet chorus before the end.

segments.title: Guitar versus banjo and the sound of Preservation Hall guitarists
segments.summary: Allen and Russell on Sales's guitar, Bud Scott and Ory's band using guitar, and the dynamics of old bands.

segments.title: Clarinet harmony, 'Dixieland' as a label and Bunk's complaints about his band
segments.summary: Clarinet harmony versus independent parts, Bunk's remark on ragtime, jazz and swing, and his friction with Jim Robinson and George Lewis in New York.

segments.title: Not knowing the tune: 'Breeze' at Preservation Hall
segments.summary: Jim Robinson as melody carrier, and a night when the band struggled with a request.

segments.title: Playing the same chorus over again
segments.summary: Whether Preservation Hall musicians enjoy playing, and the habit of repeating set solos.

segments.title: Will the New Orleans style survive?
segments.summary: Perhonas asks if Russell sees himself as preserving the style, and Russell is discouraged by how few Johnny Dodds records are in print.

segments.title: Recording Baby Dodds on drums
segments.summary: Russell's twelve hours of Baby Dodds talking about drums, the booklet, and the idea of one expert per instrument.

segments.title: The instrument interviews: trombone, bass, trumpet, banjo and piano
segments.summary: Russell lists about twenty interviews and lessons he recorded, and the planned book with a piano chapter.

segments.title: Can young musicians learn the style from records?
segments.summary: Russell and Perhonas agree people can learn by listening, though he is not hopeful.

segments.title: Jelly's term 'legitimate' and violin players in New Orleans bands
segments.summary: The article 'Jazz in the 20s', Jelly's remarks on legitimate violinists and why bands hired a reader like Manuel Manetta.

segments.title: Do the best jazz musicians read music?
segments.summary: Why the nonreading myth does not hold for Louis or Bunk, and Bunk's advice to start with solfege.

segments.title: Buddy Bolden's training, the church and the Bass sisters
segments.summary: Disputes over whether Bolden read, church influence on early jazz, and Bolden's wife's recollections.

segments.title: Reading in ragtime and eastern bands
segments.summary: The reading versus aural-roots contrast, ragtime players like Chauvin and Turpin, and Bob Wright's ear.

segments.title: Piron, Handy and Oliver records compared to New Orleans bands
segments.summary: How eastern bands sound legitimate on record, Peter Bocage's view of Louis, and the Oliver records surprising New Orleans.

segments.title: Did leaving New Orleans change Louis's style?
segments.summary: Perhonas's communal-versus-soloist theory, Louis becoming a soloist, and Giggy Williams calling the Hot Five novelty.

segments.title: The Esquire concert, Bechet and Louis, and a tape break
segments.summary: Dick Allen on the tradition's persistence, and Russell on the Esquire concert where Bechet and Louis clashed, ending with a tape change.

segments.title: Louis as entertainer within a communal tradition
segments.summary: Perhonas argues Louis saw himself as an entertainer and that the music was a way of life.

segments.title: 'Play pretty for the people': Bunk and the entertainer's duty
segments.summary: Bill Colburn's restaurant analogy, Bunk playing any request, and Baby Dodds on music making people happy.
